text: BEHAVIOURAL SCORECARDS BEHAVIOURAL MODELS AND RISK PARAMETERS §2 · BEHAVIOURAL SCORECARDS 2.1 The design decisions The same four as Document 04 §2, but two of them change shape. The observation point is no longer origination. It is a chosen point in the account's life — typically a month-end — at which you snapshot everything known about it. The observation window is the period before the observation point over which behavioural variables are computed. Conventionally 6 or 12 months. This is new; an application model has no such window because there is no prior behaviour. The outcome window is the period after the observation point over which the target is measured. Typically 12 months, shorter than for an application model because a live account's risk horizon is shorter and its data refreshes continuously. The target is usually ever-90+ within the outcome window, as before. But note the subtlety: accounts that are already delinquent at the observation point need separate treatment — either excluded, or modelled separately, because predicting default for an account already at 60 DPD is a different problem with a different base rate. 🧮 The timeline, which is worth being able to draw: an account originated in January 2024, observed at 31 December 2024, with behavioural variables computed over January–December 2024 and outcome measured over January–December 2025. text: COLLECTION SCORECARDS BEHAVIOURAL MODELS AND RISK PARAMETERS §3 · COLLECTION SCORECARDS 3.1 A different problem entirely Document 02 §10.2 and Document 03 §4.2 established the economics: cure probability collapses from around 55% in the 1–30 bucket to 15% at 31–60 to 8% at 61–90, while cost per account pursued rises. Collections capacity is a hard constraint. So the collection model's job is not to predict default. Most delinquent accounts will resolve one way or another regardless of what the model says. Its job is allocation: which accounts get which treatment, given that you cannot give every account every treatment. 📘 The target is cure, not default — the probability that an account in bucket n returns to current within a defined window. This is the mirror image of the application model's target, and getting the sign right is a surprisingly common stumble. 3.2 The distinction that separates a good collections model from a mediocre one 🔴 Propensity is not the same as treatability, and optimising for the first wastes the budget. A model that ranks accounts by probability of cure will put at the top the accounts most likely to cure — which are disproportionately the accounts that would have cured anyway, without a call. Working those accounts produces excellent measured performance and close to zero incremental recovery. What you actually want is the accounts where the treatment changes the outcome — the difference between cure-with-contact and cure-without-contact. text: PD — FROM SCORE TO PROBABILITY BEHAVIOURAL MODELS AND RISK PARAMETERS §4 · PD — FROM SCORE TO PROBABILITY Document 04 produced a score. This section turns it into a number that can enter an arithmetic. 4.1 The inversion Document 04 §7.2 scaled log-odds into points. Reverse it: > ln(odds) = ( Score − Offset ) / Factor > PD = 1 / ( 1 + odds ) 🧮 Worked, using Document 04's parameters — Offset 501.87, Factor 28.85, from a base score of 600 at 30:1 odds with a PDO of 20. At a score of 660: ln(odds) = (660 − 501.87) / 28.85 = 158.13 / 28.85 = 5.4811 odds = e^5.4811 = 240.0 → PD = 1 / 241 = 0.415% At a score of 580: ln(odds) = (580 − 501.87) / 28.85 = 78.13 / 28.85 = 2.708 odds = e^2.708 = 15.0 → PD = 1 / 16 = 6.25% 📘 The thing to notice, and it is the whole reason scaling exists. Eighty points of score — a linear difference — is a fifteen-fold difference in PD. Score is linear in log-odds, so it is exponential in risk. A credit officer who thinks of an 80-point gap as "somewhat better" has misread the instrument by an order of magnitude, and this is the single most useful thing to explain when a scorecard is handed to a business audience. 4.2 Anchoring to central tendency The PD that falls out of the model reflects the development sample's bad rate. That sample covered particular years, a particular economy, a particular policy regime. 📘 Central tendency is the long-run average default rate for the segment — the level the PD should average to across a full cycle. text: LGD — THE WEAK LINK BEHAVIOURAL MODELS AND RISK PARAMETERS §5 · LGD — THE WEAK LINK Document 03 §6.2 called LGD the weakest-evidenced component of every Indian retail ECL model. This section is why, and what to do about it. 5.1 The definition and the computation > LGD = 1 − Recovery Rate, where the recovery rate is the discounted, cost-net recovery as a proportion of exposure at default. Both adjectives carry weight. 🧮 Worked — and the gap between the naive and correct answers is the point. An account defaults with EAD of ₹5,00,000. Recoveries: ₹1,50,000 at month 12 and ₹2,00,000 at month 30. Workout costs of ₹40,000 at month 6. Discount at the effective interest rate, 15%. Discount factors: Month 6 (0.5 yr): 1 / 1.15^0.5 = 0.9325 Month 12 (1.0 yr): 1 / 1.15 = 0.8696 Month 30 (2.5 yr): 1 / 1.15^2.5 = 0.7051 Present values: Recoveries: (₹1,50,000 × 0.8696) + (₹2,00,000 × 0.7051) = ₹1,30,440 + ₹1,41,020 = ₹2,71,460 Costs: ₹40,000 × 0.9325 = ₹37,300 Net: ₹2,71,460 − ₹37,300 = ₹2,34,160 Recovery rate = ₹2,34,160 / ₹5,00,000 = 46.8% → LGD = 53.2% Now the naive version. Undiscounted, ignoring costs: (₹1,50,000 + ₹2,00,000) / ₹5,00,000 = 70% recovery → LGD = 30.0%. ⚠️ Thirty percent versus fifty-three percent — a 23-percentage-point difference, on identical cash flows. Applied across a portfolio this is the difference between adequate and severely deficient provisioning, and it arises entirely from two adjectives. text: EAD AND CREDIT CONVERSION FACTORS BEHAVIOURAL MODELS AND RISK PARAMETERS §6 · EAD AND CREDIT CONVERSION FACTORS 6.1 Term loans — nearly solved For an amortising loan, EAD at a future default date is the scheduled outstanding balance, adjusted for two things: - Prepayment, which reduces it — and which, per §4.4, became more likely for floating-rate retail from January 2026. - Capitalised amounts, which increase it. Note Document 02 §6.3: penal charges since 1 April 2024 are charges, not capitalised interest, which is precisely a rule about not letting EAD inflate on a deteriorating account. This is the easy parameter and it rarely repays much modelling effort. 6.2 Revolving facilities — where the work is 📘 Credit Conversion Factor. The proportion of the currently undrawn limit expected to be drawn by the time of default. > EAD = Current drawn + ( CCF × Undrawn limit ) 🧮 The assumption, from Document 03 §6.3. A card with a ₹2,00,000 limit and ₹60,000 drawn has ₹1,40,000 undrawn. At a 40% CCF: EAD = ₹60,000 + (0.40 × ₹1,40,000) = ₹1,16,000 — nearly double the current balance. 🧮 Now the realised outcome. Suppose that account defaults twelve months later with ₹1,52,000 drawn. The realised CCF is: > (₹1,52,000 − ₹60,000) / (₹2,00,000 − ₹60,000) = ₹92,000 / ₹1,40,000 = 65.7% ⚠️ A 40% assumption against a 65.7% outcome understates EAD by about ₹36,000 on a single account — roughly 31% of the assumed exposure. snippet: §7 · PUTTING THE THREE TOGETHER 7.1 The identity, and what it is not > Expected Loss = PD × LGD × EAD This is the Basel formulation: a single-period, through-th
text: PUTTING THE THREE TOGETHER BEHAVIOURAL MODELS AND RISK PARAMETERS §7 · PUTTING THE THREE TOGETHER 7.1 The identity, and what it is not > Expected Loss = PD × LGD × EAD This is the Basel formulation: a single-period, through-the-cycle, regulatory quantity. ECL under IFRS 9 and the 2026 Directions is a different object built from the same three parts: | | Basel EL | IFRS 9 / ECL | |:--|:--|:--| | PD | Through-the-cycle | Point-in-time, forward-looking | | Horizon | 12 months | 12 months (Stage 1) or lifetime (Stages 2 and 3) | | LGD | Downturn | Expected, unbiased | | Discounting | None | Discounted at the effective interest rate | | Scenarios | Single | Probability-weighted across multiple macro scenarios | | Floors | — | Product-wise prudential floors | 🔴 So "we already compute PD, LGD and EAD for Basel, so ECL is a small extension" is wrong in five distinct ways, and being able to enumerate them is a clean demonstration of understanding both frameworks. The three parameters are inputs to both; almost nothing else is shared. 7.2 The three numbers that must reconcile At any reporting date, a bank running the full apparatus produces three different loss figures on the same book: 1. text: VALIDATING THE PARAMETERS BEHAVIOURAL MODELS AND RISK PARAMETERS §8 · VALIDATING THE PARAMETERS Document 04 §12 validated a scorecard's ranking. Parameters need different tests, because a parameter is a level claim, not a ranking claim. 8.1 PD backtesting The test: within each rating grade or score band, compare predicted PD against realised default rate over the outcome period. The instrument: a binomial test per grade, asking whether the realised count is consistent with the predicted probability given the number of accounts. Supplemented by the calibration tests of Document 04 §10.2 — and remember the direction: a high Hosmer–Lemeshow p-value means the model passes. ⚠️ The power problem, which you should volunteer. In a grade with a predicted PD of 0.4% and 2,000 accounts, the expected default count is eight. The binomial test has almost no power to distinguish 0.4% from 0.6% at that sample size. PD backtesting in high-quality grades is statistically weak, and a "pass" there means very little. Multi-period tests that accumulate evidence across years are the standard partial remedy. 8.2 LGD and EAD backtesting Harder, for reasons §5.5 established. Realised LGD is observable only on completed workouts, and there are few of them. Realised CCF only on accounts that actually defaulted, and only where the undrawn denominator was meaningful. ✅ So the validation discipline shifts from statistical testing to three other things, and naming them is a better answer than pretending the tests are strong: 1. Behavioural beats application on the same population, because past repayment on the same obligation is the best proxy available — but the populations differ, so the Ginis are not comparable. 2. The strongest behavioural variables are about change, not level — which is also why they map naturally onto SICR. 3. Collections should optimise uplift, not propensity. A distressed borrower draws down — so PD, LGD and EAD all move adversely together, which is what makes revolving credit the most dangerous retail asset. 9. title: THE THREE LOSS NUMBERS
snippet: §1 · THE THREE LOSS NUMBERS At any reporting date after April 2027, a bank carries three different loss figures on the same portfolio. Document 05 §7.2 introduc
text: THE THREE LOSS NUMBERS ECL, IFRS 9 AND CAPITAL §1 · THE THREE LOSS NUMBERS At any reporting date after April 2027, a bank carries three different loss figures on the same portfolio. Document 05 §7.2 introduced them; here is the map. | | IRAC provision | ECL | Capital / RWA | |:--|:--|:--|:--| | Question | What do the rules require? | What do we expect to lose? | What could we lose unexpectedly? | | Basis | Asset classification ladder | PD × LGD × EAD, discounted, probability-weighted | Exposure × risk weight | | Horizon | — | 12-month or lifetime by stage | 12-month notionally | | PD flavour | — | Point-in-time, forward-looking | Through-the-cycle in principle; not used at all under SA | | Sits in | P&L and balance sheet | P&L and balance sheet | Capital adequacy computation | | From 01-04-2027 | Superseded for banks by ECL | ACPIR Directions, 2026 | Capital Charge Directions, 2026 | 📘 The distinction that keeps this straight, and it is worth saying out loud until it is automatic. Expected loss is a cost of doing business — you price for it and you provision for it. Unexpected loss is a risk — you cannot price for it because you do not know when it comes, so you hold capital against it. Provisions absorb the average; capital absorbs the surprise. ⚠️ The India-specific fact underneath all of §7, and it is the single most important structural thing to know about Indian bank capital: the RBI has implemented only the Standardised Approach for credit risk. Issued with a Statement on Feedback Received, following draft directions of 7 October 2025. Scope. Commercial banks excluding small finance banks, payments banks and local area banks; plus the corresponding new banks and SBI. Co-operative banks are outside it. All-India financial institutions have their own separate directions. NBFCs already operate under Ind AS 109 and their own IRACP Directions, 2025. title: MACRO SCENARIOS AND PROBABILITY WEIGHTING
snippet: §3 · MACRO SCENARIOS AND PROBABILITY WEIGHTING 3.1 What the Directions require ECL must incorporate forward-looking information, including macroeconomic forecas
text: MACRO SCENARIOS AND PROBABILITY WEIGHTING ECL, IFRS 9 AND CAPITAL §3 · MACRO SCENARIOS AND PROBABILITY WEIGHTING 3.1 What the Directions require ECL must incorporate forward-looking information, including macroeconomic forecasts. Specifically: - A bank shall use multiple scenarios, each representing the relationship between the key components of ECL and the relevant macroeconomic variables. - The probability weight assigned to each scenario is determined by the bank, taking into account historical experience and expert judgement, subject to oversight under the bank's approved governance framework. - Assumptions, scenario choices, weights and overlays must be documented and defensible as reasonable and supportable. 3.2 Why probability-weighting is not the same as running a central case 🧮 Worked, and this is the single most valuable piece of arithmetic in this document. A segment's modelled ECL under three scenarios: | Scenario | Weight | ECL (₹ crore) | Contribution | |:--|--:|--:|--:| | Upside | 10% | 70 | 7.0 | | Baseline | 60% | 100 | 60.0 | | Downside | 30% | 180 | 54.0 | | Probability-weighted ECL | | | ₹121 crore | The baseline alone gives ₹100 crore. The probability-weighted answer is ₹121 crore — 21% higher. 📘 Why, and the reason is structural rather than a quirk of these numbers. Losses are convex in the macroeconomic variable: they rise faster in a downturn than they fall in an upturn. Defaults have a floor near zero but no ceiling. So the average of the ECLs across scenarios exceeds the ECL computed at the average scenario. 🔴 T

text: EIR AND DISCOUNTING ECL, IFRS 9 AND CAPITAL §4 · EIR AND DISCOUNTING 4.1 What the Directions require 📘 Effective interest rate. The rate that exactly discounts estimated future cash flows through the expected life of the instrument to its gross carrying amount, determined at initial recognition. snippet: §5 · THE PRUDENTIAL FLOORS 5.1 What they are 📘 A prudential floor is a minimum provision that applies regardless of what the bank's model produces. Where IFRS
text: THE PRUDENTIAL FLOORS ECL, IFRS 9 AND CAPITAL §5 · THE PRUDENTIAL FLOORS 5.1 What they are 📘 A prudential floor is a minimum provision that applies regardless of what the bank's model produces. Where IFRS 9 is principle-based, the RBI has added product-wise minimum provisioning floors as regulatory backstops. [VERIFY — figures from commentary, not paragraph-level reading] - Stage 1: reported at 0.40% for standard corporate and retail exposures. - Stage 2: reported at a minimum of 1% of Stage 2 exposure. - Stage 3: floors varying by asset class and duration of default, set so that ECL cannot produce a lower provision than the existing IRAC schedule. - Applied at product level, across retail, corporate, MSME, agriculture and real estate. Banks argued for lower floors during consultation. The RBI held. 5.2 Where the floor binds, worked 🧮 Two segments, each with ₹10,000 crore of Stage 1 exposure. Prime home loans. Modelled 12-month PD 0.35%, LGD 20%. Modelled ECL = 0.35% × 20% = 0.07% → ₹7 crore. Floor at 0.40% → ₹40 crore. The floor binds, at roughly 5.7 times the model's output. Unsecured personal loans. Modelled 12-month PD 4.0%, LGD 85%. Modelled ECL = 4.0% × 85% = 3.40% → ₹340 crore. Floor at 0.40% → ₹40 crore. The model binds, comfortably. 🔴 Three consequences, and the third is the one worth carrying. One — in your best segments the model is decorative. Document 05 §7.2 stated this; here is the arithmetic. text: TRANSITION — THE DAY-ONE ADJUSTMENT ECL, IFRS 9 AND CAPITAL §6 · TRANSITION — THE DAY-ONE ADJUSTMENT 6.1 The mechanism 📘 The transitional adjustment amount is the difference between the ECL required as at 1 April 2027 — computed on the balance sheet position at 31 March 2027 — and the provisions held under the existing norms at 31 March 2027. That difference is added back to Common Equity Tier 1 capital, and the impact on profitability and capital adequacy may be spread over a four-year period, FY2027-28 through FY2030-31, ending 31 March 2031. [VERIFY] The exact year-by-year add-back profile — whether the unwind is straight-line at 25% a year or a declining schedule — I have not confirmed from the Directions. The four-year window and the CET1 add-back mechanism are confirmed; the profile is not. 6.2 Worked 🧮 A bank with ₹1,00,000 crore CET1 and ₹6,50,000 crore RWA — a CET1 ratio of 15.38%. At 31 March 2027 it holds ₹8,000 crore of provisions under the existing norms. Its computed ECL at 1 April 2027 is ₹11,000 crore. Transitional adjustment = ₹3,000 crore. Without the arrangement, that ₹3,000 crore hits CET1 on day one. CET1 becomes ₹97,000 crore and the ratio falls to 14.92% — a 46 basis point drop overnight, before tax effects. title: HOW THE TWO FRAMEWORKS INTERACT
snippet: §8 · HOW THE TWO FRAMEWORKS INTERACT Both land on 1 April 2027. That is deliberate, and the interaction is where understanding shows. 8.1 The mechanical link Pr
text: HOW THE TWO FRAMEWORKS INTERACT ECL, IFRS 9 AND CAPITAL §8 · HOW THE TWO FRAMEWORKS INTERACT Both land on 1 April 2027. That is deliberate, and the interaction is where understanding shows. 8.1 The mechanical link Provisions reduce the carrying amount of the asset. A higher ECL means a lower net exposure, which means lower RWA for the same loan. So an increase in provisions simultaneously: - Reduces CET1, through the P&L charge — the numerator of the capital ratio falls. - Reduces RWA, through the smaller net exposure — the denominator falls too. 📘 The numerator effect dominates, substantially, because the provision comes off capital rupee-for-rupee while it comes off RWA only after the risk weight is applied. A ₹100 crore additional provision costs ₹100 crore of CET1 and saves the risk weight applied to ₹100 crore of exposure — say ₹75 crore of RWA at 75%, which at a 9% requirement releases only about ₹6.75 crore of capital. Net cost roughly ₹93 crore. So provisioning is expensive in capital terms, and the partial offset is real but small. 8.2 Procyclicality — the structural concern Put the two frameworks together and trace a downturn. Macro forecasts worsen → PIT PDs rise → scenario weights shift toward the downside → Stage 2 migration accelerates, and each migrating account's allowance multiplies by the 2.7× or more of §2.4 → ECL rises sharply → CET1 falls → capital ratios tighten → the bank restricts lending → the downturn deepens. ⚠️ This is the well-known procyclicality of expected-loss provisioning, and India has now adopt

As-at date: 29 July 2026. Tags per Document 00. --- HOW TO READ THIS DOCUMENT Documents 03 to 06 measured a portfolio and valued it at a point in time. This one asks the question a board actually asks: what happens to us if things go badly, and do we have enough capital to survive it? It is also the document that connects your work to the room where decisions get made. Vintage curves and WoE tables do not go to a board. Stress test results and capital plans do. If you want to understand what the senior people in a risk function spend their time on, it is largely this. Read §2 carefully and be able to reproduce the capital stack from memory. It is the most reliably asked factual content in this document, and getting India's numbers right — which differ from Basel's — is a small, cheap credibility win. > The one sentence that organises this document > > ECL asks what do we expect to lose across all scenarios? snippet: §1 · WHY STRESS TESTING EXISTS 1.1 The gap that provisions do not cover Document 06 §3 established that ECL is a probability-weighted expectation across scenari
text: WHY STRESS TESTING EXISTS STRESS TESTING AND CAPITAL PLANNING §1 · WHY STRESS TESTING EXISTS 1.1 The gap that provisions do not cover Document 06 §3 established that ECL is a probability-weighted expectation across scenarios. That is the right way to compute an expected value. It is the wrong way to answer a survival question. 📘 The distinction, stated as cleanly as I can put it: - ECL takes the downside scenario and multiplies it by 30%. It answers what do we expect to lose on average? - A stress test takes the downside scenario and asks what if this simply happens? — weight 100%, no averaging. Both are correct for their purpose. Provisions absorb the expected; capital absorbs the unexpected; a stress test sizes the unexpected. 🧮 Return to Document 06 §3.2's numbers. Probability-weighted ECL was ₹121 crore. But the downside scenario alone produced ₹180 crore. The ₹59 crore difference between the provision you carry and the loss you would actually suffer is what capital is for. That single comparison is the cleanest available explanation of why a bank needs both, and it is worth being able to draw. 1.2 The three kinds of exercise | Type | Question | Direction | |:--|:--|:--| | Sensitivity analysis | What if this one variable moves? | One factor at a time | | Scenario analysis | What if this coherent set of conditions occurs? | Many factors, internally consistent | | Reverse stress testing | What would it take to break us? | Starts from the failure and works backwards | ⚠️ Sensitivity analysis is easy and mostly uninformative, because

India's numbers differ from Basel's, and knowing that difference is a cheap and reliable signal of familiarity. 2.1 The requirements | Component | India | Basel III global minimum | |:--|--:|--:| | Minimum CET1 | 5.5% | 4.5% | | Minimum Tier 1 | 7.0% | 6.0% | | Minimum total CRAR | 9.0% | 8.0% | | Capital conservation buffer (CET1) | 2.5% | 2.5% | | Countercyclical buffer (CET1) | 0% – 2.5%, currently 0 | 0 – 2.5% | | D-SIB surcharge (CET1) | 0.20% – 1.00% by bucket | — | 📘 India runs a full percentage point above Basel on total CRAR — 9% against 8% — and correspondingly higher on CET1 and Tier 1. This is a long-standing conservatism, and it is the direct reason the system's reported CRAR of 17.7% (Document 01 §5.1) sits so far above requirement. 🧮 The effective requirement, worked. For a non-D-SIB bank: CET1 of 5.5% + 2.5% CCB = 8.0%. Total CRAR of 9.0% + 2.5% = 11.5%. Even the most demanding institution carries roughly 5.8 percentage points of CRAR headroom over its requirement. ✅ Which is the answer to "is the Indian banking system well capitalised?" Not "yes." snippet: §3 · THE RBI'S MACRO STRESS TEST Published twice yearly in the Financial Stability Report, and the single best worked example of a stress test available to you
text: THE RBI'S MACRO STRESS TEST STRESS TESTING AND CAPITAL PLANNING §3 · THE RBI'S MACRO STRESS TEST Published twice yearly in the Financial Stability Report, and the single best worked example of a stress test available to you — because it is public, current and quantified. 3.1 How it is constructed Scenarios. A baseline derived from the RBI's own projections, plus two adverse scenarios of increasing severity, built on macro variable paths — GDP growth, inflation, interest rates, exchange rate, current account. Transmission. Macro variables are mapped to bank-level asset quality through fitted relationships, projecting GNPA ratios, provisions, profitability and capital ratios forward over a defined horizon. Output. Projected GNPA and CRAR under each scenario, plus the count of banks breaching minimum requirements. 3.2 The June 2026 results From Document 01 §5.1, now read as a stress exercise rather than as portfolio facts: | Measure | Result | |:--|:--| | GNPA, March 2026 actual | 1.8% — a multi-decadal low | | GNPA, baseline projection to March 2028 | 1.9% | | GNPA, adverse scenarios | 3.8% – 4.1% | | Severe credit shock sensitivity | GNPA at 8.1%; four banks, 12% of system assets, breach minimum CRAR | | NBFCs — 174 entities tested | CRAR 22.8% → 21.7% baseline, 20.9% severe; GNPA 2.3% → 5.4% worst case; 11 NBFCs below the 15% CRAR requirement | 📘 Three things to read off this, which is more than most people extract from it. text: A BANK'S OWN STRESS TEST STRESS TESTING AND CAPITAL PLANNING §4 · A BANK'S OWN STRESS TEST 4.1 The transmission chain Everything in a credit stress test is one chain, executed in order. Being able to recite it — and to name which link is weakest — is a good demonstration of understanding. > Macro scenario → risk parameters → asset quality → provisions → P&L → capital → ratios Link by link: 1. Macro scenario. A coherent, internally consistent path for GDP growth, inflation, policy rate, unemployment or a proxy, exchange rate, and asset prices — for retail, particularly property and gold prices, per Document 01 §2.2. 2. Macro to parameters. The satellite models. PD rises; LGD rises as collateral values fall; EAD rises as distressed borrowers draw down. Document 05 §6.2's point lands hard here: all three move adversely together. 3. Parameters to asset quality. Higher PDs produce more SMA and NPA formation, projected through Document 03 §4's transition matrices under stressed roll rates. 4. Asset quality to provisions. Post-April-2027, through the ECL machinery — which means Stage 2 migration, and Document 06 §2.4's 2.7× cliff. 5. Provisions to P&L. Provision charge, plus lost interest income on Stage 3 exposures accruing on net carrying amount, plus any margin compression in the scenario. 6. P&L to capital. Reduced or negative profit reduces retained earnings and therefore CET1. 7. Capital to ratios. title: REVERSE STRESS TESTING
parentTitle: CREDIT-RISK // STRESS TESTING AND CAPITAL PLANNING
snippet: §5 · REVERSE STRESS TESTING 5.1 What it is 📘 Conventional stress testing starts with a scenario and computes the outcome. Reverse stress testing starts with th
text: REVERSE STRESS TESTING STRESS TESTING AND CAPITAL PLANNING §5 · REVERSE STRESS TESTING 5.1 What it is 📘 Conventional stress testing starts with a scenario and computes the outcome. Reverse stress testing starts with the outcome — the bank becomes non-viable — and works backwards to find the scenarios that produce it. Then it asks: how plausible is that, and what would we see coming? 5.2 Why it is the most valuable exercise and the least done 🔴 Conventional stress testing has a built-in bias toward comfortable answers, and the mechanism is worth being explicit about. The scenarios are chosen by the institution being tested. Nobody proposes a scenario that breaks their own bank, because doing so invites a supervisory conversation nobody wants. So severity is calibrated, consciously or not, to a level the institution survives — and the exercise then confirms resilience, which is what everyone expected. Reverse stress testing removes that degree of freedom by fixing the outcome. You cannot calibrate your way out of it. The output is a set of scenarios that break you, and the discussion becomes about their plausibility and about early warning indicators — which is a far more useful conversation than "we passed." ✅ The three outputs a good reverse stress test produces: 1. The binding constraint. Which exposure, concentration or funding dependency breaks first. Often not the one management expected. 2. The early indicators. If that scenario were beginning, what would move first? Those become monitoring triggers. 3. The contingency actions

text: ICAAP STRESS TESTING AND CAPITAL PLANNING §6 · ICAAP 6.1 The three pillars, and what Pillar 2 is actually for | Pillar | Content | |:--|:--| | Pillar 1 | Minimum capital for credit, market and operational risk — formula-driven, Document 06 §7 | | Pillar 2 | Supervisory review, and the bank's own Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process | | Pillar 3 | Market discipline through disclosure | 📘 Pillar 1 covers three risks with prescribed formulas. Pillar 2 covers everything else — and "everything else" is where most of the risks that have actually killed banks live. 6.2 What ICAAP must address beyond Pillar 1 - Concentration risk — single borrower, group, sector, geography. Pillar 1's standardised approach is blind to it: a portfolio of one hundred loans to the same sector and one hundred diversified loans carry identical RWA. This is the largest single Pillar 1 gap. - Interest rate risk in the banking book (IRRBB) — economic value and earnings sensitivity to rate movements. - Liquidity and funding risk, interacting with capital. - Business and strategic risk — the risk that the business model stops working. - Reputational risk — and Document 02 §10.4's conduct rules are the live channel for this in retail lending. - Model risk — now with an explicit framework pending, per Document 04's opening. - Residual credit risk — where credit risk mitigation does not perform as assumed. snippet: §7 · CAPITAL PLANNING 7.1 The cycle > Business plan → RWA projection → capital demand → capital supply → gap → reallocate or raise Business plan. Growth by prod
text: CAPITAL PLANNING STRESS TESTING AND CAPITAL PLANNING §7 · CAPITAL PLANNING 7.1 The cycle > Business plan → RWA projection → capital demand → capital supply → gap → reallocate or raise Business plan. Growth by product, segment and geography. RWA projection. Apply the risk-weight framework of Document 06 §7 to the planned book. From 1 April 2027 this becomes materially harder, because risk weight now depends on LTV bands, borrower-level system-wide housing loan counts, and twelve-month transactor status — so projecting RWA requires projecting the composition of the book at a granularity most planning processes have never needed. Capital demand. Required ratio × projected RWA, plus buffers, plus the ICAAP add-on for Pillar 2 risks, plus management's own operating headroom above requirement. Capital supply. Opening capital, plus retained earnings, less dividends, plus any planned issuance — and AT1 and Tier 2 instruments count toward total CRAR but not CET1. The gap. If demand exceeds supply, three levers: raise capital, reduce growth, or change the mix. ✅ The third lever is where a credit risk analyst earns their keep, and it is worth saying so. Growing a 30%-risk-weight mortgage book consumes roughly a quarter of the capital of growing a 125%-risk-weight personal loan book of the same size. Mix is a capital decision before it is a commercial one, and the person who can quantify that trade sits in a different conversation from the person who reports delinquency. 7.2 RAROC — and a result that surprises people 📘 Risk-Adjusted Retur

snippet: §8 · THE 2027 COMPLICATION — STRESS TESTING UNDER ECL Everything in §4 changes character on 1 April 2027, and this section is where Documents 06 and 07 fuse. 8.
text: THE 2027 COMPLICATION — STRESS TESTING UNDER ECL STRESS TESTING AND CAPITAL PLANNING §8 · THE 2027 COMPLICATION — STRESS TESTING UNDER ECL Everything in §4 changes character on 1 April 2027, and this section is where Documents 06 and 07 fuse. 8.1 The new dominant channel Under IRAC, a stress scenario hit capital through NPA formation — accounts crossing 90 days, attracting provisions on the classification ladder. Slow, rule-bound, and lagging by construction. Under ECL, the dominant channel becomes Stage 2 migration, and it is faster and larger. 🔴 Why. Three compounding reasons: 1. SICR triggers at 30 DPD as a rebuttable presumption — sixty days earlier than NPA classification. 2. It also triggers on a significant increase in lifetime PD, which in a deteriorating macro scenario happens to accounts that are fully current. No delinquency required at all. 3. Each migrating account's allowance multiplies by 2.7× or more on the Document 06 §2.4 arithmetic, and by more again for long-tenor exposures. 📘 Put together: under ECL, provisions rise before any account misses a payment. A worsening macro forecast raises lifetime PDs, pushes accounts across the SICR threshold, and multiplies their allowances — on a book that is still performing perfectly. ⚠️ This is the structural change stress testing must absorb, and it is why Document 06 §6.3 insisted the real change in April 2027 is the variance, not the level. A stress model built on the IRAC transmission chain — macro to NPA to provision — will materially understate the speed and size of the capital impact under ECL

The gap between ₹121 crore and ₹180 crore is what capital is for. 2. India's stack: CET1 5.5%, Tier 1 7%, CRAR 9%, plus a 2.5% CCB, plus a D-SIB surcharge of 0.20% to 0.80%. One point above Basel throughout. 3. A buffer is meant to be used. Breaching it restricts distributions; it is not a breach of the minimum. 4. The CCyB has never been activated in India — the trigger is the credit-to-GDP gap, and India prefers targeted sectoral tools instead. 5. The FSR's 8.1% is a sensitivity, not a scenario, and the NBFC results are the more consequential half. 6. The weakest link in any Indian retail stress test is the macro-to-default satellite model, because the only recent downturn was contaminated by moratoria. 7. Report the P&L, not just the ratio. A bank can be capital-adequate through a stress and still lose a year's earnings. 8. Reverse stress testing is the only exercise you cannot calibrate your way out of. 9. Pillar 1 is blind to concentration. That is Pillar 2's largest single job. 10. RAROC, not margin. The 30%-weighted mortgage beats the 125%-weighted personal loan at a third of the spread — which explains Document 01's whole growth pattern. 11. It exists because the gap between knowing credit risk and being useful in a credit risk team is almost entirely craft — knowing which cut to run first, knowing that your number has to tie to finance's number, knowing that a Gini improvement means nothing to a business head and a swap set means everything. None of that is in a textbook, and all of it is visible within a week to anyone already doing the job. Read it differently from the others. Documents 03 to 06 you read to be able to reason. This one you read to be able to behave — to walk into a portfolio review and know what is expected of you. > The one sentence that organises this document > > Nobody in the room wants your analysis. They want a decision they can defend — and your job is to compress a week of work into the three sentences that change what someone does on Monday. ---

snippet: §1 · THE SHAPE OF THE JOB 1.1 Three modes, and they compete for the same hours Run. The recurring machine. Monthly packs, regulatory returns, model monitoring,
text: THE SHAPE OF THE JOB THE ANALYST'S DESK §1 · THE SHAPE OF THE JOB 1.1 Three modes, and they compete for the same hours Run. The recurring machine. Monthly packs, regulatory returns, model monitoring, provision computation. Non-negotiable deadlines, and it will consume as much time as you let it. Build. Models, scorecards, new segmentations, the ECL implementation. High-value, and always the first thing sacrificed when Run overruns. Answer. The ad hoc question. "Why is Bihar personal loan delinquency up?" "What happens to RWA if we grow the gold book by 30%?" Unpredictable, usually urgent, and — this is the part people miss — this is where your reputation is actually made. The monthly pack is expected; the fast, correct, well-framed answer to a hard question is what gets you into the next conversation. ⚠️ The failure mode of every junior analyst is letting Run consume everything, then reporting at appraisal time that they produced the pack on time for twelve months. That is a description of a process, not of a contribution. Automate Run ruthlessly so you have hours for Answer — and this, concretely, is where your technical background converts into career advantage in a way that a pure-domain colleague cannot match. 1.2 The rhythm | Cadence | Work | |:--|:--| | Daily | Bounce and mandate failure tracking; collections dashboard refresh | | Weekly | Bucket balances, flow, collections productivity; escalations | | Monthly | The portfolio pack; transition matrices; model monitoring — PSI and CSI; provision computation; r

text: THE REPORTING PACK THE ANALYST'S DESK §3 · THE REPORTING PACK Four standing artefacts. Each answers a different question for a different audience, and knowing which is which is most of the skill. 3.1 The origination pack — what are we writing? Audience: business heads, credit policy, and whoever owns growth. - Volume and value by product, channel, geography, ticket band — with month-on-month and year-on-year. - Approval rate, and the decomposition into policy declines and score declines (Document 04 §5.1). - Score distribution of approvals, against the development sample. - Deviation rate by approving authority (Document 02 §6.1). - Average ticket, tenor, LTV, FOIR. - PSI on the applicant population. 📘 This is the only pack that is genuinely forward-looking. Everything else reports on business already written. Deviation rate and approval-rate drift move before delinquency does, which is exactly what makes them worth a senior person's attention. 3.2 The portfolio pack — what do we hold? Audience: risk committee, CRO, finance. - Outstanding by product, segment, vintage. - Delinquency by bucket, by value and by account, with the rupee numerator alongside every ratio (Document 03 §2.2). - Transition matrix and terminal-roll implied NPA formation (Document 03 §4.3). - Vintage curves, quarterly refresh, cut by channel and score band. - Stage distribution and provision — Stage 1 / 2 / 3, with movement analysis. - Concentration: top exposures, geography, sector. 3.3 The collections pack — are we recovering? text: THE INVESTIGATION PLAYBOOK THE ANALYST'S DESK §6 · THE INVESTIGATION PLAYBOOK A worked diagnosis, in order. This sequence is the most transferable thing in this document. The trigger. The monthly pack shows personal loan PAR 31–90 up from 1.9% to 2.4%. Step 1 — Is it real? Before anything else, rule out artefacts. - Did the book shrink? A falling denominator raises a ratio with no new stress (Document 03 §2.2). Check the rupee numerator. - Did the DPD calculation or a system change? Ask. - Did a reporting cadence change? Document 03 §8.4 — from 1 July 2026 bureau data refreshes four times a month, and any velocity-based attribute or bureau-sourced delinquency view changes meaning at that boundary. - Is it seasonality? Document 02 §2.4 — check the same month last year, not just last month. Step 2 — Numerator or denominator? Decompose the ratio. If the numerator in rupees is flat and the ratio rose, the story is about the denominator and there is no credit finding. Step 3 — Cohort or flow? Cut delinquency by origination month at a common months-on-book. - Concentrated in recent cohorts → underwriting or sourcing. Continue to Step 4. - Spread evenly across all cohorts → collections or environment. Continue to Step 6. This single cut answers the question everyone in the room is actually arguing about, and it should be the first chart you produce. Step 4 — Which segment? title: PRESENTING TO PEOPLE WHO WILL NOT READ THE APPENDIX
snippet: §8 · PRESENTING TO PEOPLE WHO WILL NOT READ THE APPENDIX 8.1 Three rules One — inverted pyramid. Conclusion first, then support, then method. Academic order is
text: PRESENTING TO PEOPLE WHO WILL NOT READ THE APPENDIX THE ANALYST'S DESK §8 · PRESENTING TO PEOPLE WHO WILL NOT READ THE APPENDIX 8.1 Three rules One — inverted pyramid. Conclusion first, then support, then method. Academic order is exactly backwards for this audience. If the room reads only your first line, it should still get the finding. Two — one chart, one message. If you cannot write the message as a sentence in the chart title, the chart is not ready. "PAR 31–90 by origination cohort" is a label. "Cohorts written after September are deteriorating at twice the rate at the same age" is a message. Three — the number that matters, not the number that is interesting. Gini went from 0.38 to 0.44 is interesting to you. The swap set is worth ₹X crore of avoided loss at constant approval rate is what matters to them (Document 04 §11.2). 8.2 Presenting uncertainty without becoming useless You will often have to say something with weak evidence — Document 05 §5.5 on LGD, Document 06 §3.3 on macro relationships. 🔴 The failure mode is hedging until the statement carries no information. "It could go either way depending on assumptions" is technically true and operationally worthless. ✅ The structure that works: a point estimate, a range, a driver, and a trigger. > "Central case is 3.2%. Plausible range 2.6% to 4.5%, and the width is driven almost entirely by LGD, where we have 140 completed workouts. title: WORKING WITH THE REST OF THE BANK
snippet: §9 · WORKING WITH THE REST OF THE BANK Business. They are not the enemy and they are not stupid. They are optimising volume under a target you did not set. Brin
text: WORKING WITH THE REST OF THE BANK THE ANALYST'S DESK §9 · WORKING WITH THE REST OF THE BANK Business. They are not the enemy and they are not stupid. They are optimising volume under a target you did not set. Bring them findings they can act on, and bring them early — a partner switched off in month two is a smaller conversation than one switched off in month eight after ₹200 crore of bad business. Finance. They own the number that goes to the market. Reconcile before you publish, always (§2.3). From 2027 they become your closest working relationship, because ECL sits in the P&L and the provision is jointly owned. IT and data engineering. Every snapshot, every feed, every point-in-time table depends on them. Being the risk analyst who can write the query, read the schema and specify the change precisely is worth more than any single model you will build — and it is the clearest place your technical background compounds. Collections. They will tell you what the data cannot: that a particular geography has become impossible to visit, that a partner's customers are unreachable, that a treatment has stopped working. Field intelligence leads the data by weeks. Spend time on the collections floor; almost nobody in analytics does, and it shows in their models. Internal audit and validation. Adversarial by design, and correctly so. Make their job easy — documented, reproducible, reconciled — and they become an ally who finds your errors before a supervisor does. ---

title: THE FIRST NINETY DAYS
snippet: §10 · THE FIRST NINETY DAYS If you take a seat in a retail credit risk function, this is the order. Weeks 1–2 — the map. What products, what volumes, what chann
text: THE FIRST NINETY DAYS THE ANALYST'S DESK §10 · THE FIRST NINETY DAYS If you take a seat in a retail credit risk function, this is the order. Weeks 1–2 — the map. What products, what volumes, what channels, what systems. Read the last four board risk committee packs; they tell you what the institution worries about. Read the credit policy. Weeks 3–4 — the data. Do monthly snapshots exist and how far back? Does the mart reconcile to the ledger? Where are origination-date attributes stored? Can you get borrower-level aggregation? Write down what does not exist. That list is your first contribution. Weeks 5–8 — reproduce. Take last month's published pack and rebuild every number yourself. You will find discrepancies. Understanding them teaches you the data model faster than any documentation, and finding one real error in your first two months establishes you permanently. Weeks 9–12 — one finding. Run the §6 playbook on the segment with the worst trend. Produce one finding, quantified in rupees, with a recommendation. One finding that changes a decision is worth more than three months of faultless pack production, and it is what people will remember when they describe you to someone else. ✅ And the thing to resist: the urge to build a model in month one. You do not yet know the data, the definitions, the policy history or the mix. A model built in that state will be wrong in ways you cannot see, and it will be the thing you are known for. ---

title: HOW TO USE THIS DOCUMENT
snippet: Every self-test for this set, in one place. Cover the answer. Say it out loud. Fifteen minutes at a time. As-at date: 29 July 2026. All answers reflect the set
text: HOW TO USE THIS DOCUMENT THE INTERROGATION Every self-test for this set, in one place. Cover the answer. Say it out loud. Fifteen minutes at a time. As-at date: 29 July 2026. All answers reflect the set as written; regulatory items carry the same tags and the same expiry risk as the documents they came from. --- HOW TO USE THIS DOCUMENT This is the only document in the set meant to be opened out of order. The protocol, and it matters more than the content: 1. Cover the answer. Physically, or with your hand on a phone screen. Reading a question and its answer together produces recognition, which feels like knowing and is not. 2. Say it out loud. Not in your head. The gap between what you can recognise and what you can produce under mild pressure with someone watching is enormous, and speaking is the only way to close it. This is the whole reason this document exists separately. 3. Fifteen minutes. Longer and you stop retrieving and start reading. 4. Mark every miss. A small dot beside the question. On the third pass, work only the dotted ones. 5. Space it. Same section again after two days, then a week, then a fortnight. Massed repetition on one evening produces almost nothing durable. ⚠️ One honest warning. Some answers here are three sentences long. In a real room the answer is often one sentence plus a pause. The long-form answer is for learning; the short form is for the interview. When you can give the long answer fluently, practise cutting it to its first sentence and stopping. ---

title: DOCUMENT 01 — THE INDIAN RETAIL BOOK
snippet: §2 · DOCUMENT 01 — THE INDIAN RETAIL BOOK Give the shape of the Indian retail book in three sentences. ₹170.2 lakh crore across roughly 688 million accounts, gr
text: DOCUMENT 01 — THE INDIAN RETAIL BOOK THE INTERROGATION §2 · DOCUMENT 01 — THE INDIAN RETAIL BOOK Give the shape of the Indian retail book in three sentences. ₹170.2 lakh crore across roughly 688 million accounts, growing 16.6%. Home loans are a third of the value and 3% of the accounts. Gold, personal, cards and consumer durables are under a quarter of the value and more than two-thirds of the accounts. Why is "retail credit grew 16.6%" a nearly useless statement? Because within it gold grew 50.4% and credit cards grew 0.0%. The aggregate averages seven products with almost nothing in common. Break the gold loan growth into its causes. Four. Collateral revaluation — ticket size up 52% on flat volumes. The tiered LTV relaxation to 85% under ₹2.5 lakh. Reclassification of agri-gold into retail, about a third of the book. And genuine substitution away from unsecured. Only the last is borrower demand. Gold delinquency fell sharply. Why should you not be reassured? Falling delinquency during a bullion price rally is a collateral effect, not a credit-quality effect. A borrower whose pledged gold has appreciated will always find a way to repay or refinance rather than surrender it. What is the real gold loan exposure, then? A sustained price correction. Loans written near the peak sit closest to collateral value, trigger margin calls, and convert a benign book quickly. The RBI's June 2026 FSR flags exactly this, noting gold growth at a 42.4% CAGR driven by repeat borrowers. State the gold loan LTV tiers and the bullet repayment rule. 85

title: DOCUMENT 02 — THE LOAN LIFECYCLE
snippet: §3 · DOCUMENT 02 — THE LOAN LIFECYCLE Name the ten stages. Sourcing; application and identity; fraud screening; credit assessment; decision and pricing; sanctio
text: DOCUMENT 02 — THE LOAN LIFECYCLE THE INTERROGATION §3 · DOCUMENT 02 — THE LOAN LIFECYCLE Name the ten stages. Sourcing; application and identity; fraud screening; credit assessment; decision and pricing; sanction and documentation; disbursal; servicing and monitoring; collections; classification, recovery and write-off. State the upstream principle. The cost of fixing a problem rises by roughly an order of magnitude at each stage downstream. Almost every collections problem is an underwriting problem that arrived late, and almost every underwriting problem is a sourcing problem that arrived late. What is structurally wrong with DSA sourcing? Commission is paid on disbursal, so the agent's economic interest ends the day the money moves while the lender carries the next sixty months. How do you control it? Not with a rule — with measurement. DSA-level vintage analysis with a standing cut-off policy. V-CIP versus OTP-based e-KYC — what's the difference and why does it matter? V-CIP is treated on par with face-to-face onboarding. OTP e-KYC is not — it carries transaction limits and requires the relationship to be regularised. It's a real constraint on what a digital lender can write. Why is KYC a credit risk topic and not just compliance? The identity record is the join key to the bureau, to deduplication, and to collections reachability. Weak identifiers produce low bureau hit rates, undetected duplicate exposure and unreachable accounts — which present as model problems and are onboarding problems. Distinguish credit risk, firs

text: DOCUMENT 03 — THE MEASUREMENT LAYER THE INTERROGATION §4 · DOCUMENT 03 — THE MEASUREMENT LAYER Name the three views and what each can do. Cohort — vintage curves, answers whether the business we're writing is getting better. Flow — roll rates and transition matrices, answers what's happening now. Stock — snapshot delinquency, reports and cannot diagnose. Why can a snapshot never diagnose? It confounds underwriting quality, seasoning and growth dilution, and cannot separate them. Do the growth-dilution arithmetic. ₹1,000 crore seasoned at 4.0% is ₹40 crore. Add ₹600 crore of new business at 0.5%, ₹3 crore. Total ₹43 crore on ₹1,600 crore — 2.7%. The ratio improved from 4.0% with nothing changed. What does vintage analysis do that nothing else does? It groups by origination month and plots against months on book rather than calendar time, which removes seasoning and growth dilution simultaneously. Three things you read off a vintage chart. Level at a common MOB — the clean quality signal. Shape — where the deterioration starts. The maturity point where it flattens, which sets the minimum performance window for a scorecard. A cohort is worse from MOB 2. What kind of problem is it? Fraud or channel compromise. First-payment and early-payment default. A cohort is worse only from MOB 6. What kind? Genuine credit deterioration. Which single vintage cut is worth most? title: DOCUMENT 04 — SCORECARDS
snippet: §5 · DOCUMENT 04 — SCORECARDS What does a scorecard do, in one sentence? It ranks. The cut-off decides, and the cut-off is a statement of business appetite, not
text: DOCUMENT 04 — SCORECARDS THE INTERROGATION §5 · DOCUMENT 04 — SCORECARDS What does a scorecard do, in one sentence? It ranks. The cut-off decides, and the cut-off is a statement of business appetite, not a modelling output. Name the four design decisions before any data. Bad definition, performance window, sample window, exclusions. How would you set the bad definition from evidence rather than convention? Build the roll-rate matrix and place it at the point of no return — where cure probability has collapsed and eventual default is largely determined. How do you set the performance window? To the product's maturity point off the vintage curves. For Indian unsecured retail, usually 12 to 18 months. Which exclusions matter most, and why? Confirmed fraud and first-payment defaults, because first-party fraud in the bad population teaches the model to predict something that isn't credit risk. Why is out-of-time the split that matters? Because a random holdout shares the training period's population, policy regime and economy — it detects overfitting and nothing else. OOT answers the question production actually asks. A large in-time to OOT gap means what? Population instability more than overfitting. Investigate with CSI rather than regularising harder. Write the WoE and IV formulas. WoE = ln(%Good / %Bad), using distribution shares not rates. IV contribution = (%Good − %Bad) × WoE, summed across bins. What's the sign-convention trap? With ln(%Good/%Bad), positive WoE means better than average. Many shops use ln(%Bad/%Goo

title: DOCUMENT 05 — BEHAVIOURAL MODELS AND PARAMETERS
snippet: §6 · DOCUMENT 05 — BEHAVIOURAL MODELS AND PARAMETERS Why does a behavioural model out-discriminate an application model? Past repayment behaviour on the same ob
text: DOCUMENT 05 — BEHAVIOURAL MODELS AND PARAMETERS THE INTERROGATION §6 · DOCUMENT 05 — BEHAVIOURAL MODELS AND PARAMETERS Why does a behavioural model out-discriminate an application model? Past repayment behaviour on the same obligation is the best available proxy for future repayment on it. Nothing in an application file competes. Why can't you compare their Ginis? The behavioural model is built on survivors — a different population with a lower base rate. What kind of variable dominates a behavioural model? Change, not level. Utilisation drift beats utilisation. DPD trend beats maximum DPD. New-trade velocity beats trade count. Which is also why they map naturally onto SICR, a change concept. What is endogeneity in this context? If a good score triggers a limit increase and the limit changes utilisation, the model is partly predicting the consequences of its own decisions. Partial defence: a small randomised group exempt from score-driven actions. What's the target of a collections scorecard? Cure, not default. Why is a propensity ranking the wrong tool? Because the top of it is accounts that would have cured anyway. You want uplift — where the treatment changes the outcome — which needs variation in treatment, ideally a randomised no-contact holdout. Convert a score of 660 to a PD, using Offset 501.87 and Factor 28.85. ln(odds) = (660 − 501.87) / 28.85 = 5.4811. Odds ≈ 240. PD = 1/241 = 0.415%. text: DOCUMENT 06 — ECL, IFRS 9 AND CAPITAL THE INTERROGATION §7 · DOCUMENT 06 — ECL, IFRS 9 AND CAPITAL Name the instrument, its number, its date and its effective date. RBI (Commercial Banks – Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition) Directions, 2026 — RBI/DOR/2026-27/398, dated 27 April 2026, effective 1 April 2027. Who is in scope and who isn't? Commercial banks excluding small finance banks, payments banks and local area banks, plus SBI and the corresponding new banks. Co-operative banks are outside. AIFIs have separate directions. Why does India's SA-only choice matter for everything you've learned? Because there's no IRB option, your PD and LGD models don't touch regulatory capital. They drive provisions, pricing and internal decisions; RWA comes from a prescribed table. Give the three stages and their allowances. Stage 1, no significant increase in credit risk — 12-month ECL. Stage 2, SICR but not credit-impaired — lifetime ECL. Stage 3, credit-impaired — lifetime ECL, and interest accrues on the net carrying amount. What's the single most common conceptual error about SICR? Treating it as an absolute test. It's relative to origination. A loan originated at 8% and now at 10% may not have suffered a SICR; one originated at 0.3% and now at 1.2% almost certainly has. And the operational consequence? You must retain each account's origination-date PD forever. A bank that didn't cannot do quantitative SICR at all. Name the SICR triggers. title: DOCUMENT 07 — STRESS TESTING AND CAPITAL PLANNING
snippet: §8 · DOCUMENT 07 — STRESS TESTING AND CAPITAL PLANNING ECL versus a stress test, in one line each. ECL multiplies the downside by its probability and asks what
text: DOCUMENT 07 — STRESS TESTING AND CAPITAL PLANNING THE INTERROGATION §8 · DOCUMENT 07 — STRESS TESTING AND CAPITAL PLANNING ECL versus a stress test, in one line each. ECL multiplies the downside by its probability and asks what we expect to lose. A stress test asks what happens if the downside simply occurs. Where does capital fit in that? In the gap. Probability-weighted ECL was ₹121 crore; the downside alone was ₹180 crore. The ₹59 crore difference is what capital is for. Recite India's capital stack. CET1 5.5%, Tier 1 7.0%, total CRAR 9.0% — a full point above Basel throughout — plus a 2.5% capital conservation buffer, a countercyclical buffer of 0 to 2.5% currently at zero, and a D-SIB surcharge of 0.20% to 1.00%. Effective CET1 requirement for SBI? 5.5 + 2.5 + 0.80 = 8.30%. HDFC Bank 8.10%, ICICI 7.95%. System CRAR is 17.7%. So? Roughly 5.8 percentage points of headroom over the most demanding requirement — which is why the FSR's severe scenario puts only four banks, 12% of assets, below minimum. Is a buffer a minimum? No. It's capital you're expected to use in bad times. Breaching it restricts discretionary distributions — dividends, buybacks, bonuses — on a sliding scale; it isn't a breach of the requirement. And the practical problem with that design? Banks are reluctant to use buffers because a visible drawdown invites market punishment, so buffers behave more like minimums than intended. Answer — the fast, correct, well-framed response to a hard question. The monthly pack is expected; that isn't. What is the most expensive data failure in a lending institution? Holding only current-state delinquency instead of monthly snapshots. Without point-in-time history there's no vintage curve, no transition matrix, no backtest and no stability index — and it can't be reconstructed later. Why is modelling with current attributes against historical outcomes dangerous? Silent leakage. The underwriting decision used the old value; querying today gives the new one. It produces suspiciously good models. Why must your total tie to finance's total? Because if the total is wrong the composition is probably wrong too, and every subsequent risk number gets questioned — correctly. Name the five numbers for a credit committee. Gross flow into the 1–30 bucket with its terminal-roll conversion; the 1–30 to 31–60 roll by segment; MOB 6 cumulative 90+ for the three newest mature cohorts by channel; approval and deviation rate by authority; PSI and CSI on the live scorecard. What do CIMS and DAKSH do? CIMS is the RBI's returns platform, with statutory and supervisory returns migrated in phases through 2023–2025; it also carries digital lending app reporting. title: THE TWELVE MOST-FUMBLED FACTS
snippet: §10 · THE TWELVE MOST-FUMBLED FACTS Work these until they are automatic. Each is a free win and each is commonly got wrong. 1. A high Hosmer–Lemeshow p-value is
text: THE TWELVE MOST-FUMBLED FACTS THE INTERROGATION §10 · THE TWELVE MOST-FUMBLED FACTS Work these until they are automatic. Each is a free win and each is commonly got wrong. 1. A high Hosmer–Lemeshow p-value is a PASS. 2. An NPA upgrades only on payment of the ENTIRE arrears — not on DPD falling below 90, not on partial payment. 3. SICR is relative to origination, not an absolute risk level. 4. Penal CHARGE, not penal interest, and not capitalised. 5. V-CIP equals face-to-face; OTP-based e-KYC does not. 6. India's minimum CRAR is 9%, not Basel's 8%. 7. A buffer is meant to be used; breaching it restricts distributions, not compliance. 8. Technical write-off removes the asset, not the liability. 9. Growth dilutes delinquency — 4.0% becomes 2.7% with nothing improved. 10. The FSR's 8.1% is a sensitivity, not a scenario. 11. Lifetime PD is built from declining marginal hazards — 8.14%, not 15%. 12. India is Standardised-Approach only — your PD and LGD don't drive regulatory capital. ---

title: THE HOSTILE MOCK

text: THE HOSTILE MOCK THE INTERROGATION §12 · THE HOSTILE MOCK Ten questions in sequence, as a sceptical risk manager would actually ask them. Do this one out loud, standing up, without notes. 1. "Tell me what's happening in Indian retail credit right now." 2. "You said gold grew 50%. Is that a good thing?" 3. "Our GNPA is 1.8%. Why should I be worried about anything?" 4. "Our personal loan delinquency improved last quarter. Convince me it's real." 5. "How would you know this book was turning before the NPA number moved?" 6. "We're getting a new scorecard. The vendor says Gini 0.52. Should I buy it?" 7. "Explain ECL to me as if I run the business, not the risk function." 8. "What breaks in April 2027 that isn't breaking now?" 9. "You have thirty seconds with the CEO. What's the one number?" 10. "What's the weakest part of our whole risk framework, and don't be diplomatic." ⚠️ On question 10. The right answer for an Indian retail book is almost certainly LGD, and the reasoning is Document 05 §5.5: it needs completed workouts, the book grew too fast to have many, excluding incomplete workouts biases toward fast resolutions which are the good ones, and there's no observed downturn in which collateral values fell and recovery data was cleanly captured. Saying that reads as experience. Claiming everything is robust reads as someone who has only read about it. ---

title: THE CLOSING NOTE
snippet: §13 · THE CLOSING NOTE You now have eight documents of substance and one of interrogation. A few honest things about what that does and doesn't give you. What i
text: THE CLOSING NOTE THE INTERROGATION §13 · THE CLOSING NOTE You now have eight documents of substance and one of interrogation. A few honest things about what that does and doesn't give you. What it gives you. A defensible, current, quantified account of the Indian retail credit market and the frameworks over it — with dates, with sources, and with the open questions marked rather than papered over. Most candidates in this market have the vocabulary. Far fewer have the arithmetic, and almost none have the arithmetic attached to the right instrument on the right date. What it doesn't. It won't make you someone who has run a portfolio through a cycle. That happens the first time a number you published moves and you have to explain why in a room where it costs somebody something. Reading is preparation; the artefacts are evidence; the seat is the qualification. The thing that will age fastest. Every [VERIFY] and [DRAFT] tag in this set. The model risk guidance, the recovery agent amendments, the prudential floor percentages, the LTV bucket boundaries. Check them before you use them. And when something in here turns out to be wrong — it will — that's the finding. Bring it back and we'll fix the document. And the one habit underneath all of it, which outlasts every rule in these pages: whose book, which date, which definition, and does it net off write-offs. Four questions, ten seconds. They will catch most of the errors that make a good analyst look careless, and asking them out loud in a room is itself the signal.

text: What this set is, and what it replaces THE ROLE AND THE MAP What this set is, and what it replaces You own ten volumes of AI-engineering material — 228 chapters, roughly 177,000 words. It is good material. It is also organised like a syllabus: foundations, then prompting, then retrieval, then agents, and so on outward. That ordering is honest for a curriculum and useless for a job, because no job arrives in that order. A job arrives as one customer with one broken process and a deadline. So this set does something different. It takes the technical substance of those ten volumes, cuts what a Forward Deployed Engineer will never touch, deepens what an FDE lives inside daily, adds the entire customer-facing half that the textbooks never covered — and reorders all of it along the arc of one real deployment, start to finish. You are not studying nine documents. You are shipping one system, and learning everything at the moment the system demands it. There are nine documents plus this map. Read them in order. Each one picks up where the last put the deployment down. ---

text: PART I — THE ROLE THE ROLE AND THE MAP PART I — THE ROLE What a Forward Deployed Engineer actually is An FDE is an engineer who embeds inside a customer's organisation and makes a product work in that customer's real, hostile, undocumented environment. The role combines software development with domain understanding and direct collaboration with end users, and typically spans the whole lifecycle of a system — requirements analysis, design, implementation, integration, and deployment. The compressed version: a normal engineer ships features to an anonymous user base. An FDE ships an outcome to a named customer, and owns whatever stands between the product and that outcome. Whatever stands in the way becomes your job. Not "that's the platform team's problem." Not "file a ticket." Yours. The 20/80 Law — the most important sentence in this document Getting a demo working in a sandbox is maybe 20% of the job. The other 80% is navigating enterprise SSO, legacy ETL pipelines, regulatory constraints like SOC 2, HIPAA and FedRAMP, data residency, and the politics of getting production credentials out of a customer's security team. Sit with that, because it should reorganise how you value your own study time. Almost everyone teaching themselves AI engineering right now is optimising the 20%. They are getting very good at prompts, RAG chunking strategies, and agent frameworks — the part that produces a working demo. That skill has become abundant. It is not what gets you hired and it is definitely not what gets a deployment

snippet: PART II — THE SPINE Every document in this set advances one deployment through one arc. The arc has seven movements, and it is the same arc in every FDE job you
text: PART II — THE SPINE THE ROLE AND THE MAP PART II — THE SPINE Every document in this set advances one deployment through one arc. The arc has seven movements, and it is the same arc in every FDE job you will ever hold. 1. Discovery. Find out what the customer actually does, as opposed to what they told the salesperson. Find the real process, the real people, the real data, the real politics. 2. Scoping. Choose the narrowest slice that produces visible value and is actually shippable. Say no to four things. This movement kills more deployments through cowardice than any technical failure. 3. The demo. Build the 20%. Make it real enough to be believed, honest enough to survive questions. 4. Integration archaeology. Discover that the data is in a 1990s system, half the fields are free text, the schema doc is wrong, and the person who knew how it worked left in 2019. This is where the 80% begins. 5. Hardening. Evals, security, auth, monitoring, cost control, failure handling. The unglamorous work that converts a demo into a system a regulated institution will run. 6. Production and adoption. Ship it. Watch nobody use it. Find out why. Fix that. Adoption is a separate problem from deployment and it is not your product manager's job while you are on site. 7. Handover and pattern-back. Make it survivable without you, and carry what you learned back to the product team. The best FDEs are the eyes of the product team — if an FDE's work isn't influencing what gets built next, the role is being misused. Documents 01 through 08

snippet: PART IV — CREDIT RISK, IN ONE SITTING You cannot deploy into a lender while nodding blankly at their vocabulary. This is the minimum. It is enough to hold a rea
text: PART IV — CREDIT RISK, IN ONE SITTING THE ROLE AND THE MAP PART IV — CREDIT RISK, IN ONE SITTING You cannot deploy into a lender while nodding blankly at their vocabulary. This is the minimum. It is enough to hold a real conversation; the depth arrives in context as the deployment proceeds. What a lender is actually doing A lender has one core question about every application: if we give this person money, what do we expect to lose? The industry decomposes it into three numbers. - PD — Probability of Default. How likely is this borrower to stop paying? A number between 0 and 1. - LGD — Loss Given Default. If they do default, what fraction of the money do we fail to recover? Secured lending has low LGD (you can seize the collateral). Unsecured personal loans have high LGD. - EAD — Exposure at Default. How much will actually be outstanding at the moment things go wrong? For a term loan that's predictable. For a credit line it isn't, because distressed borrowers draw down their remaining credit right before defaulting. And the equation that ties them: Expected Loss = PD × LGD × EAD That is the whole engine. Everything a credit risk team does is estimating, monitoring, or defending one of those three numbers. If you remember one formula from this entire set, remember that one — you can hold a serious conversation with Dan Whitfield on the strength of it.
